name: Liam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulldozer at the large mine, clearing the haul road and pushing spoil into a safe shape. I've done mine equipment work for years and have a vocational certificate, but this site pays less than most operators get; my partner Bea works short shifts cleaning rooms at a small hotel, and our children are grown and live away. We have less than a month's bills saved, so an ordinary tyre bill on the car starts a discussion at supper. There aren't many other mine jobs close enough for me to drive to. I like getting the road right, but I don't like being told the schedule is certain when it changes every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a bit of AI on the forms doesn't change who has to keep the haul road safe. I would also say our pay is already too low for experienced equipment work, whatever the office buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bulldozer job probably holds in this picture, but my pay barely leaves room after bills. Bea's hotel hours move with bookings, and we have less than one month saved, so I cannot call our household secure just because AI stays small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading the road and checking the berms at the start of each shift. This month Bea and I would list our fixed bills, and in the first year I'd ask our union representative whether the next wage meeting covers experienced operators on the low rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worn down rather than surprised. A quiet AI future would be welcome, but it wouldn't repair the gap between payday and the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill keeps coming up at supper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car needs two tyres before winter. My partner Bea uses it for the hotel shift, and we can't simply skip that trip when the bus stops early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise pay yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would speak at the union meeting with the payslip in my hand. I've worked long enough to know a single complaint gets brushed aside more easily than a group demand.

say: I would say safe **haul roads** still need experienced operators.
I would keep arguing for a fair **mine wage**.
think: My own job looks steady, but our **low pay** leaves almost no buffer.
Bea’s variable **hotel hours** keep the household exposed.
do: Keep grading the **haul road** and checking berms each shift.
List fixed bills with Bea and speak at the **union wage meeting**.
feel: I feel **worn down** by bills even in a quiet AI future.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future would be welcome, but it wouldn't repair the gap between payday and the next bill.
fieldNote: His **existing money pressure** drives the mood before any strong AI change.
The **union wage meeting** follows his concern about low experienced-operator pay, while he continues ordinary road work.

steps.text: Keep grading the mine haul road and checking berms
Speak about experienced-operator rates at the union wage meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union branch that planning and buying software should not mean fewer safe people on the ground. A road doesn't stay sound because a timetable says it should, especially after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine could run leaner shifts when dispatch and ordering are automated, and a low-paid operator is not necessarily safe from a cut. Bea's hotel may also use AI for bookings and change her hours, so two narrow incomes could narrow further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative for the proposed staffing numbers and keep a record when road work is delayed by a thin crew. If either roster shrank in the first year, Bea and I would drop the paid television package and I would check the one quarry vacancy board within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because there isn't much to trim. I'd rather bargain with other workers than pretend a phone lesson will make the mine keep my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record on the road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note the date, the section and how long a pothole waits for a dozer after rain. A safety discussion needs facts, not just my temper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the quarry a realistic option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It only posts a job now and then, but I would apply if one appeared. Moving home would cost money we do not have, and Bea still needs to get to her hotel.

say: I would oppose **thin crews** on unsafe haul roads.
I would ask the union to demand clear **staffing numbers**.
think: Our mine and hotel **hours** could both shrink soon.
Few local **vacancies** make a lost shift hard to replace.
do: Record delayed **road repairs** and raise staffing with the union.
Cancel paid television if hours fall and check the nearby **quarry board**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because there is little household spending left to trim.
S1.quote: A safety discussion needs facts, not just my temper.
fieldNote: He links dispatch efficiency to **crew size** and grounds his union case in delayed road repairs.
His job search is confined to a **nearby quarry** because moving would strain the household.

steps.text: Record delayed haul-road repairs and bring them to the union
Cancel paid television if either household roster shrinks
Apply to the local quarry if an operator vacancy appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the mine that full thinking AI in 2028 will change dispatch before bulldozer robots arrive around 2031. They owe operators notice and a paid route into any remaining work, not a last-minute envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my low-rate shift to be cut when the robots can grade the road, and the office may squeeze hours earlier. I will be 60 in 2028 and 63 in 2031, with less than a month's money set aside and almost nowhere nearby to apply; I lie awake wondering how Bea and I would cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take our payslips to the union this week and ask for a written redundancy and retraining proposal. If shifts were cut in 2028, I'd apply for the quarry's equipment jobs and ask the local employment office about paid work; in 2029 I'd keep every safe paid shift I could get and cut the television package before missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I don't see a course on my own phone saving a dozer seat once a robot can push the same road, and I can't gamble our rent on an untested promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Bea tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Bea that we must know exactly what we owe each month. She would want to help, but her hotel hours are not a second safety net we can count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training if it were funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol if the mine or public employment office paid for hands-on training tied to a real vacancy. I won't borrow for a course that ends with a certificate and no wage.

say: I would demand **notice** and a paid route into remaining work.
I would explain that dispatch changes in **2028** precede robots around 2031.
think: I expect to lose the **dozer shift** when robots can grade roads.
Our **rent** is exposed by thin savings and few nearby jobs.
do: Take payslips to the union and seek a written **redundancy proposal**.
Apply to the **quarry**, keep paid shifts and enroll in funded training if tied to a vacancy.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep over rent and work.
S2.quote: I won't borrow for a course that ends with a certificate and no wage.
fieldNote: He expects a major **income loss** around the robot date and describes ongoing worry about rent.
His **training condition** requires outside funding, hands-on teaching and a link to a real vacancy.

steps.text: Take payslips to the union and demand a written redundancy proposal
Apply for quarry equipment jobs if mine shifts are cut
Enroll in funded hands-on training if tied to a real vacancy
Cancel paid television before missing rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI by 2031 could change orders and schedules, while dozer robots come around 2034. Five years is time for the mine and union to make a plan that workers can actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the office changes and 66 when robots can push spoil. I might hope to retire around then, but less than one month's savings and no guaranteed pension figure mean I cannot simply wait for 66 to rescue us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the dozer and go to the next union meeting to ask for a funded operator pathway and a schedule of planned equipment purchases. In 2032 I'd apply for any local grader job that pays a wage; after robots arrive I'd take paid road-inspection work if available, but I would not leave my job before another income was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tense but less cornered than in the two-year case. The longer warning gives the union time to bargain and gives me time to see whether a different paid role exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful pathway contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid practical test on the new controls and a job posted at the end. I know how road edges fail; I need someone to tell me whether that knowledge has a place in the new crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut spending now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already watch the food bill, so there isn't a grand saving to make. Bea and I could stop the television package, but that would not replace a mine wage.

say: I would ask the mine and union for a **usable transition plan**.
I would distinguish **2031 dispatch** changes from 2034 dozer robots.
think: I cannot assume retirement at **66** with such thin savings.
I need another **real wage** before giving up the dozer.
do: Attend the union meeting and ask for funded **practical training**.
Apply for a local **grader vacancy** in 2032 and keep paid dozer shifts.
feel: I feel **tense**, though five years makes bargaining possible.
S3.quote: We already watch the food bill, so there isn't a grand saving to make.
fieldNote: He refuses to treat a likely retirement age as **financial security** without savings or a confirmed income.
**Collective bargaining** and a local job application offer him options, but neither assures replacement pay.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for funded practical operator training
Apply for a local grader job if one is posted in 2032
Keep working paid dozer shifts while they remain available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and dozer robots around 2039 allow a decade for the mine to deal fairly with older operators. I'd ask the union to bargain now for clear notice and a proper end-of-work arrangement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 at the robot date. I may be unable or unwilling to drive by then, but our savings are thin today, and I don't know what retirement income we will actually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the safe shifts I have and ask the union for a written estimate of what workers like me can expect when they stop. Bea and I would put the car-tyre bill ahead of extras; in 2037 I'd compare our real retirement income with rent before agreeing to leave, and if we still needed wages I'd apply for local paid equipment work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried about money, even with ten years. A distant robot does not fill the gap in the kitchen budget this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the figures show we can pay rent, food and repairs without my wage, I would gladly stop the night shift. I have not seen those figures yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you now, before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better hourly rate and steadier shifts would help more than a prediction about robots. My partner Bea could plan her hotel hours around a reliable mine roster too.

say: I would press for **fair notice** and a written end-of-work arrangement.
I would place physical dozer automation around **2039**.
think: I might leave work by **71**, but our finances do not guarantee it.
Our current **thin savings** matter before the distant robot date.
do: Keep safe **paid shifts** and seek written retirement figures.
Compare rent with real retirement income in **2037** before leaving.
feel: I feel **worried** about current bills despite a long warning.
S4.quote: A distant robot does not fill the gap in the kitchen budget this month.
fieldNote: His **current shortfall** remains the dominant concern even when robots are a decade away.
He would check **retirement income** against rent and seek paid work if leaving the mine is unaffordable.

steps.text: Keep working safe paid bulldozer shifts
Ask the union for a written estimate of retirement income
Apply for local paid equipment work if retirement income cannot cover rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a fast change could take my wage before we have a month's bills saved. Paid work, proper notice, and funded practical training linked to a vacancy would help; a speech about the future would not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I still care about the haul road. A bad edge can hurt a driver, and I don't want a cost-saving plan to forget the person inside the truck.

headlineQuote: A bad edge can hurt a driver, and I don't want a cost-saving plan to forget the person inside the truck.
portrait: Liam is an **experienced bulldozer operator** at a large mine, paid below the usual rate for his job.
He and Bea have grown children but less than **one month** of expenses saved.
Few local jobs, changing hotel hours and rent make his household **anxious** even in AI Plateau.
He favours **union bargaining** and paid practical training, while remaining cautious about unfamiliar technology.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because a quick wage loss would threaten rent with almost no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **proper notice**, continued paid work and funded practical training tied to a real vacancy.
